facts.statement: Leedsichthys is an extinct genus of fish.
facts.quote: taxon: Leedsichthys

facts.statement: The genus Leedsichthys was described by Arthur Smith Woodward in 1889.
facts.quote: authority: Woodward, 1889

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Leedsichthys problematicus.
facts.quote: type_species: Leedsichthys problematicus

facts.statement: Leedsichthys notocetes was proposed as a synonym of Leedsichthys problematicus in 1999.
facts.quote: synonyms: *L. notocetes? Martill et al., 1999

facts.statement: Leedsichthys fossils range from the Callovian to the Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Callovian-Tithonian~

facts.statement: Leedsichthys was a pachycormid fish that lived in the oceans during the Middle to Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: Leedsichthys is an extinct genus of pachycormid fish that lived in the oceans of the Middle to Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: The genus was named after British collector Alfred Nicholson Leeds in 1889.
facts.quote: Especially important were the finds by the British collector Alfred Nicholson Leeds, after whom the genus was named "Leeds' fish" in 1889.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys fossils have been found in England, France, Germany, Argentina, and Chile.
facts.quote: Leedsichthys fossils have been found in England, France, Germany, Argentina and Chile.

facts.statement: A second species, Leedsichthys notocetes, was named in 1999 based on Chilean finds but was later considered indistinguishable from Leedsichthys problematicus.
facts.quote: In 1999, based on the Chilean discoveries, a second species was named Leedsichthys notocetes, but this was later shown to be indistinguishable from L. problematicus.

facts.statement: Large parts of Leedsichthys consisted of cartilage that did not fossilize.
facts.quote: Large parts consisted of cartilage that did not fossilize.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys fed mainly on plankton, filtering it from seawater using gill rakers equipped with delicate bone plates.
facts.quote: The gill arches were lined by gill rakers, equipped with a unique system of delicate bone plates that filtered plankton from sea water as the main food source.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys was part of a lineage of large filter-feeding fish that lived from the Middle Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Along with its close pachycormid relatives Bonnerichthys and Rhinconichthys, Leedsichthys is part of a lineage of large-sized filter-feeders that swam the Mesozoic seas for over 100 million years, from the middle Jurassic until the end of the Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: If pachycormids are an early branch of Teleostei, Leedsichthys would be the largest known teleost fish.
facts.quote: Pachycormids might represent an early branch of Teleostei, the group most modern bony fishes belong to; in that case Leedsichthys is the largest known teleost fish.

facts.statement: On August 22, 1888, Othniel Charles Marsh concluded that fossils found by Leeds were the skull bones of a giant fish rather than dinosaur armor.
facts.quote: On 22 August 1888, the American dinosaur expert Professor Othniel Charles Marsh visited Leeds' farm at Eyebury and quickly concluded that the presumed dinosaurian armour in fact represented the skull bones of a giant fish.

facts.statement: Arthur Smith Woodward examined the specimens within two weeks of Marsh's visit and published a formal description in 1889.
facts.quote: Within two weeks British fish expert Arthur Smith Woodward examined the specimens and began to prepare a formal description published in 1889.

facts.statement: The specific epithet problematicus was chosen because the remains were so fragmented they were hard to recognize and interpret.
facts.quote: The fossils found by Leeds gave the fish the specific epithet problematicus because the remains were so fragmented that they were extremely hard to recognize and interpret.

facts.statement: Woodward changed the genus name to Leedsia in 1890, resulting in the name Leedsia problematica.
facts.quote: Woodward therefore in 1890 changed the genus name to Leedsia, resulting in a Leedsia problematica.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was found in the Oxford Clay Formation of the Callovian, about 165 million years old.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, BMNH P.6921, had been found in a layer of the Oxford Clay Formation dating from the Callovian, about 165 million years old.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of 1133 disarticulated skeletal elements, mostly fin ray fragments, likely from a single individual.
facts.quote: It consists of 1133 disarticulated elements of the skeleton, mostly fin ray fragments, probably of a single individual.

facts.statement: In January 1915, Leeds sold a pectoral fin and the remainder of a skeleton with 904 elements to the Hunterian Museum, Glasgow.
facts.quote: In January 1915 Leeds sold specimens GLAHM V3362, a pectoral fin, and GLAHM V3363, the remainder of the same skeleton with 904 elements, to the Hunterian Museum, Glasgow.

facts.statement: In September 1901, Friedrich von Huene mistakenly identified Leedsichthys remains as tail spikes of Omosaurus, but Leeds corrected him the same year.
facts.quote: In September 1901, they were examined by the German palaeontologist Friedrich von Huene, who identified them as tail spikes, Schwanzstacheln, of Omosaurus, the second time Leedsichthys remains were mistaken for stegosaurian bones; Leeds himself was able to disabuse von Huene the same year.

facts.statement: In 2001, students discovered a major British specimen nicknamed "Ariston" after a 1991 washing machine commercial.
facts.quote: In 2001, students at the Dogsthorpe Star Pit discovered a major new British specimen that they nicknamed "Ariston" after a 1991 commercial for the Indesit Ariston washing machine that claimed it went "on and on and on".

facts.statement: From 2002 to 2004, Jeff Liston's team excavated the "Ariston" specimen, removing ten thousand tonnes of loam with a 15-meter overburden.
facts.quote: From 2002 until 2004 "Ariston" or specimen PETMG F174 was excavated by a team headed by Jeff Liston; to uncover the remains it was necessary to remove ten thousand tonnes of loam forming an overburden of 15 m thickness.

facts.statement: In July 1982, two groups of amateur paleontologists began digging up the same Leedsichthys skeleton at Wallücke, Germany.
facts.quote: In July 1982, Germany became an important source of Leedsichthys fossils when two groups of amateur palaeontologists, unaware of each other's activities, began to dig up the same skeleton at Wallücke.

facts.statement: Fragmentary Leedsichthys fossils were uncovered in Chile starting in 1973.
facts.quote: From 1973 onwards, fragmentary Leedsichthys fossils were uncovered in Chile.

facts.statement: A more complete specimen, SMNK 2573 PAL, was found in Chile in March 1994.
facts.quote: In March 1994, a more complete specimen was found, SMNK 2573 PAL.

facts.statement: Jeff Liston concluded that distinguishing traits of Leedsichthys notocetes were erosion artifacts, making it a junior synonym of Leedsichthys problematicus.
facts.quote: However, Liston later concluded that the presumed distinguishing traits of this species, depressions on the gill rakers, were artefacts caused by erosion; Leedsichthys notocetes would be a junior synonym of Leedsichthys problematicus.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys fossils have been found in the Callovian of England and northern Germany, the Oxfordian of Chile, and the Callovian and upper Kimmeridgian of France.
facts.quote: The fossil remains of Leedsichthys have been found in the Callovian of England (Oxford Clay) and northern Germany, the Oxfordian of Chile (El Profeta Formation & Cerro Campamento Formation), and the Callovian and upper Kimmeridgian of France (Calcaire de Creully Formation).

facts.statement: Over seventy individuals of Leedsichthys have been found, though most remains are partial and fragmentary.
facts.quote: Although the remains of over seventy individuals have been found, most of them are partial and fragmentary.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys had toothless jaws.
facts.quote: The jaws are toothless.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys possessed gill rakers that were 3 to 12 centimeters long.
facts.quote: The gill arches are equipped with rows of parallel 3-to-12-centimetre-long (1.2-to-4.7-inch-long) gill rakers

facts.statement: The small teeth on the gill rakers of Leedsichthys were directed obliquely toward the front and top.
facts.quote: The teeth or "fimbriations" are obliquely directed towards the front and the top.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys fed on plankton by filtering it from seawater using its gill rakers.
facts.quote: The rakers served to filter plankton, the main food supply of Leedsichthys, from the sea water.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys had two pectoral fins located low on its body.
facts.quote: Leedsichthys has two pectoral fins that probably were located rather low on the body.

facts.statement: The pectoral fins of Leedsichthys were large, elongated about five times their width, scythe-like, and curved 10 degrees backward at the lower end.
facts.quote: They are large, very elongated—about five times longer than wide—and scythe-like, with a sudden kink at the lower end, curving 10° to the rear.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys lacked pelvic fins and a pelvic plate.
facts.quote: Pelvic fins at the belly are lacking; also a pelvic plate is absent.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys had a large, symmetrical vertical tail fin with paired upper and lower lobes and a smaller central lobe.
facts.quote: The vertical tail fin is very large and symmetrical with paired upper and lower lobes; there is a smaller lobe in the middle protruding between them.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys did not have bony scales.
facts.quote: No bony scales are present.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys is the largest known member of the Osteichthyes (bony fishes).
facts.quote: Leedsichthys is the largest known member of the Osteichthyes or bony fishes.

facts.statement: Arthur Smith Woodward described the type specimen of Leedsichthys in 1889 and estimated its length to be around nine meters.
facts.quote: Arthur Smith Woodward, who described the type specimen in 1889, estimated specimen BMNH P.10000 to be of an around nine metre long individual

facts.statement: Growth rings in Leedsichthys remains indicate it took 21 to 25 years to reach adult size.
facts.quote: The growth ring structures within the remains of Leedsichthys have indicated that it would have taken 21 to 25 years to reach these lengths

facts.statement: A 2013 study estimated that Leedsichthys specimens aged between 19 and 40 years.
facts.quote: In 2013, Liston and colleagues estimated that the age of the five specimens (PETMG F174, NHMUK PV P10000, GLAHM V3363, NHMUK PV P6921 and NHMUK PV P10156) would have ranged between 19 and 40 years old.

facts.statement: Arthur Smith Woodward initially classified Leedsichthys in the Acipenseroidea, relating it to sturgeons.
facts.quote: Woodward initially assigned Leedsichthys to the Acipenseroidea, considering it related to the sturgeon

facts.statement: In 1905, Arthur Smith Woodward reclassified Leedsichthys into the family Pachycormidae.
facts.quote: In 1905, he changed this to the Pachycormidae.

facts.statement: Cladistic analysis places Leedsichthys as the sister species of Asthenocormus within the Pachycormidae.
facts.quote: Within the Pachycormidae, a cladistic analysis found Leedsichthys to be the sister species of Asthenocormus

facts.statement: It is debated whether Pachycormidae, including Leedsichthys, are basal Teleostei or members of a separate order Pachycormiformes sister to Teleostei.
facts.quote: Often they are considered very basal Teleostei—if so, Leedsichthys would be the largest known teleost—others see them as members of a Pachycormiformes forming the sister group of the Teleostei

facts.statement: There is a scientific debate regarding the size of Leedsichthys, with Liston arguing for much lower length estimates than earlier popular accounts.
facts.quote: Liston in his studies concluded to much lower estimates.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys problematicus was a suspension feeder that used specialized gill rakers to eat zooplankton and small animals.
facts.quote: Like the largest fish today, the whale sharks and basking sharks, Leedsichthys problematicus derived its nutrition as a suspension feeder, using an array of specialised gill rakers lining its gill basket to extract zooplankton, small animals, from the water passing through its mouth and across its gills.

facts.statement: It is unclear if phytoplankton or algae were part of Leedsichthys's diet.
facts.quote: It is less clear whether also phytoplankton, algae, were part of the diet.

facts.statement: In 2010, Liston suggested that furrows in Swiss sea floors were made by Leedsichthys spouting water to eat bottom-dwelling animals, rather than by plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: In 2010, Liston suggested that fossilised furrows discovered in ancient sea floors in Switzerland and attributed to the activity of plesiosaurs, had in fact been made by Leedsichthys spouting water through its mouth to disturb and eat the benthos, the animals dwelling in the sea floor mud.

facts.statement: A 2013 study by Liston suggested that Leedsichthys had a slow, nearly linear growth pattern.
facts.quote: Liston's 2013 study suggested a slow, nearly linear, growth.

facts.statement: A 1993 French study concluded that Leedsichthys had a high metabolism based on its bone structure.
facts.quote: A French study in 1993 of its bone structure concluded however, that the metabolism was rather high.

facts.statement: In 1986, Martill reported finding a tooth of the marine crocodile Metriorhynchus in a Leedsichthys bone.
facts.quote: In 1986, Martill reported the presence of a tooth of the marine crocodile Metriorhynchus in a bone of Leedsichthys.

facts.statement: In 2007, Liston concluded that a Leedsichthys bone containing a Metriorhynchus tooth had not healed, suggesting the crocodile scavenged the fish.
facts.quote: However, in 2007 Liston concluded the bone tissue had not in fact healed and that this was probably a case of scavenging.

facts.statement: The pliosaurid Liopleurodon was an apex predator in the Oxford Clay seas capable of attacking Leedsichthys.
facts.quote: An apex predator of the Oxford Clay seas large enough to attack Leedsichthys was the pliosaurid Liopleurodon.

facts.statement: In 1999, Martill suggested that climate change at the end of the Callovian caused Leedsichthys extinction in northern seas, with the southern Ocean serving as a refuge.
facts.quote: In 1999 Martill suggested that a climate change at the end of the Callovian led to the extinction of Leedsichthys in the northern seas, the southern Ocean offering a last refuge during the Oxfordian.

facts.statement: In 2010, Liston argued against the northern extinction theory by noting Leedsichthys fossils from the Kimmeridgian in Normandy.
facts.quote: However, in 2010 Liston pointed out that Leedsichthys during the later Kimmeridgian was still present in the north, as testified by Normandian finds.

facts.statement: Studies view Leedsichthys as the start of a lineage of large pachycormid suspension feeders that lasted into the Late Cretaceous, showing convergent evolution with baleen whales.
facts.quote: Indeed, further studies supported this, viewing Leedsichthys as the beginning of a long line of large (>2 m in length) pachycormid suspension feeders that continued to flourish well into the Late Cretaceous, such as Bonnerichthys and Rhinconichthys, and emphasising the convergent evolutionary paths taken by pachycormids and baleen whales.

facts.statement: Comparisons with living teleost fish suggest Leedsichthys could swim at speeds of 17.8 kph while maintaining oxygenation.
facts.quote: Using data from living teleost fish as a comparison, scientists discovered that Leedsichthys could have cruised along at potential speeds of 17.8 kph while still maintaining oxygenation of its body tissues.

facts.statement: Leedsichthys belongs to the parent group Asthenocorminae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Asthenocorminae

facts.statement: Leedsichthys is classified in the family Pachycormidae.
facts.quote: Family: Pachycormidae

facts.statement: Leedsichthys is classified in the class Osteichthyes.
facts.quote: Class: Osteichthyes

facts.quote: Type species: Leedsichthys problematicus
